title: Pilgrims' roads
hook: Canterbury, Santiago, Rome: people walked a long way to reach a holy place

segments.voice: Yesterday, mystery plays: the Bible acted on wagons by townspeople, with shipwrights building the ark. Your line was the bible on wagons.

Why would anyone leave home on foot to reach a grave? Part of the answer hangs from a walking stick: a scallop shell, tied on with a bit of cord. That's how you'd know someone was on the road to Santiago. Blisters, a small bag, a hat against the sun. They left home long ago, and won't sleep in their own bed for a long time yet. In Chaucer's tales, a company on horseback trades stories on the way to Canterbury. On another road, travelers climb toward Rome. Different roads, one question underneath.

Each road ended at a grave or a shrine. Rome, where tradition says Peter and Paul are buried. Santiago de Compostela, in Spain, where tradition places the tomb of James the apostle, and where the scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge. Canterbury, in England, where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in his own cathedral and then honored as a saint. People went to ask for healing, to give thanks, to do penance for a wrong, to keep a promise. Some, honestly, for the adventure: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is full of pilgrims who talk more than they pray. But the road itself mattered. Leaving home meant leaving your comfort, your title, your routine. On the road, a merchant and a farmer could sleep in the same hostel and eat the same soup, and monasteries and towns along the way took pilgrims in. Hebrews says the faithful of old confessed, in the King James Bible, "that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." A Psalm that longs for God's house blesses the one "in whose heart are the ways of them." And tradition says pilgrims sang another Psalm as they climbed toward Jerusalem: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Christians haven't all agreed about pilgrimage. Some reformers later criticized it, saying God is just as near at home. Catholic and Orthodox Christians still go, and so do others, on foot. And some walkers say the same surprising thing: the road became the prayer.
screen: `A GRAVE OR A SHRINE AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Think of a place within walking distance that means something to you: a church, a park, a grave, a tree, a friend's front door. Picture setting out without your phone in your hand, carrying one intention, thanks, a worry or a person. If you pray, pray along the way in your mind; if you don't, let each pictured step be the attention.
Pilgrims' roads. The roads to holy places like Rome, Santiago and Canterbury, walked for healing, thanks or penance, where the journey itself becomes part of the prayer.
Your line: the road is the prayer. Every road began at someone's front door. Day eight hundred forty-two, complete.

howItsDone: Christians, and others too, still walk the Camino to Santiago de Compostela, carrying a scallop shell and collecting stamps in a pilgrim passport, and pilgrims still travel to Rome, Canterbury, the Holy Land and other shrines.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or distances are given. 'They might have left home weeks ago' is a hypothetical, not a statistic; cut if needed.
Burial of Peter and Paul in Rome and the tomb of James at Santiago are given as tradition. Becket's murder in Canterbury Cathedral is history; confirm phrasing.
Psalm 122 is one of the Songs of Degrees (Psalms of Ascents), which tradition connects with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem; the teach says 'tradition says pilgrims sang'.
Psalm 84:5 KJV: 'Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them.' The gloss 'the roads up to God's house' is interpretive; confirm.
Reformers' criticism of pilgrimage (e.g. Luther, Erasmus's satire) summarized without naming; 'Catholic and Orthodox Christians still go, and so do others'; confirm.
Chaucer's pilgrims ride on horseback; the hook says 'on horseback'. Confirm.
